newsitem.title: spain: Spain sizzling mad at European olive oil plans.
newsitem.headline: Spain sizzling mad at European olive oil plans.

text.p: Spain's olive oil farmers are sizzling mad.
Their age-old industry, which has provided a lifeline to Mediterranean farmers for centuries, is being threatened by controversial European Union reforms.

Farmers say radical changes to the way subsidies are calculated will punish Spain's productive olive industry, wiping out thousands of jobs and devastating a sector vital to the survival of some parts of Spain.

"It's an outrage. They want to cut our subsidies which would mean ruin for many farmers ... they say fraud is the problem but it's just not true," said a farmer from the southern Andalusian region, which produces around 75 percent of the country's oil.

Spain prides itself on being the world's biggest olive oil producer, supplying some 700,000 tons of the world's 2 million ton total last year. The industry supports some of Spain's most hard-up areas where unemployment exceeds 30 percent.
But to keep the sector afloat, the EU spent $2 billion last year subsidising Europe's 2 million olive oil farmers in France, Greece, Italy, Portugal and Spain. Spain soaked up a third of the aid.
The Commission complains that millions are gobbled up by fraud and the sector is forecast to overproduce into the next century. Reforms are vital, it says.

The Commission enraged Spain's olive sector with reform proposals earlier this year aimed at changing the basis on which subsidies are awarded. It wants aid to be linked to the number of trees a farmer cultivates rather than production.

"The EU reforms would mean less subsidies and less jobs for Spain's farmers and would lead to lower production and an erosion in quality ... it would create fundamental social problems," said Rafael Milan, an oil specialist at the Agriculture Ministry.
Spain has complained that EU Agriculture Commissioner Franz Fischler, who is heading the reform drive, knows little about Europe's olive oil industry and should not decide its future.
"Franz Fischler doesn't have a clue about the sector. He must inform himself better about the facts," Milan said.
Farmers cite Fischler's attempt to pick an olive off a tree and eat it during a recent trip to Spain as an illustration of his ignorance.
Olives undergo a complex preparation before they are ready to eat. Picked directly from the tree, they leave a bitter taste in the mouth and give the unwitting nibbler indigestion.
If Fischler takes his proposals much further Spain says it will try to blockade them.
"We will vote against the proposals and we will join with other countries to form a minor blockade," Spain's Agriculture Minister Loyola de Palacio said in a recent magazine interview.
"We are developing a coordinated action with Mediterranean producer countries to maintain a position of unanimous rejection."
Under the current system, the Commission offers production subsidies to small and large producers at different rates, said to be the principal cause of fraud.
But Spain complains it is not a serious offender and should not be punished.

"The greatest fraud is committed by small olive oil producers, and in Italy they make up 70 percent of the sector," De Palacio said. Small producers make up just 4 percent of Spain's olive producers, the Agriculture Ministry says.
The Commission says the system should be replaced with one based on the number of trees and historic regional yields or changed to a single subsidy system.

Spain protests that subsidies based on the number of trees, the option most favoured by the European Commission, would cripple its industry, cutting vital subsidies from current levels of around 100 billion pesetas ($690 million) to as low as 30 billion pesetas ($227 million).
As a result, the sector, which provides farmers with an average of 46 million days of work a year, could see a loss of 12 million of those days, the Agriculture Ministry says.
Producers say Spain's trees yield more than other producing countries and therefore would receive more aid from the current system based on production.
Spain's long-time olive oil rival, Italy, on the other hand, should benefit from a system based on the number of trees, with its lower yielding trees.
"Spain wants to continue with the current system in which subsidies are production-based which provides a greater incentive for production and quality," Milan said.
